claim: Translin knockout mice lack both translin and trax proteins.
source: As trax protein is unstable in the absence of translin, translin KO mice are completely devoid of both proteins (Chennathukuzhi et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chennathukuzhi et al., 2003 and Yang et al., 2004

claim: Translin knockout mice display normal long-term spatial and contextual memory in water maze and fear conditioning tasks.
source: Previous behavioral characterization of these mice has revealed that they have intact long-term spatial and contextual memory assessed by the water maze and fear conditioning (Stein et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stein et al., 2006

claim: Translin knockout mice show reduced anxiety-related behavior.
source: However, behaviors from such aversive tasks need careful interpretation as translin KO mice display reduced anxiety-related behavior in addition to developmental adaptations (Chennathukuzhi et al., 2003; Stein et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chennathukuzhi et al., 2003 and Stein et al., 2006

claim: Translin knockout mice exhibit developmental adaptations.
source: However, behaviors from such aversive tasks need careful interpretation as translin KO mice display reduced anxiety-related behavior in addition to developmental adaptations (Chennathukuzhi et al., 2003; Stein et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chennathukuzhi et al., 2003 and Stein et al., 2006

claim: Hippocampal slices from translin knockout mice show similar 4-train-induced long-lasting potentiation to wildtype slices in pathway S1.
source: Hippocampal slices from translin KO mice that lack translin/trax showed similar 4-train-induced long-lasting potentiation to wildtype (WT) slices in pathway S1 (Figure 1B1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B1 with statistical analysis (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,8) = 0.03, p=0.9)

claim: 1-train stimulation following S1 stimulation fails to induce persistent potentiation in pathway S2 in translin knockout slices.
source: In pathway S2, however, 1-train stimulation following S1 stimulation failed to induce persistent potentiation in translin KO slices (Figure 1B2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B2 with statistical analysis (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,8) = 36.5, p=0.0003)

claim: Translin knockout mice show unaltered 1-train-induced short-lived potentiation when administered alone.
source: Importantly, translin KO mice did not show altered 1-train-induced short-lived potentiation when administered alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A with statistical analysis (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,8) = 0.07, p=0.8)

claim: Basal synaptic transmission measured by input-output relationship is unaltered in translin knockout mice.
source: Basal synaptic transmission measured by the input-output relationship and PPF was also unaltered in translin KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; KO: 5 ± 1.9, n = 6; WT: 3.8 ± 0.6, t-test, p=0.6, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(1,10) = 0.2, p=0.8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B with statistical analysis (t-test, p=0.6)

claim: Paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) is unaltered in translin knockout mice.
source: Basal synaptic transmission measured by the input-output relationship and PPF was also unaltered in translin KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; KO: 5 ± 1.9, n = 6; WT: 3.8 ± 0.6, t-test, p=0.6, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(1,10) = 0.2, p=0.8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C with statistical analysis (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(1,10) = 0.2, p=0.8)

claim: Translin knockout mice explored the displaced object significantly less than wildtype littermates 24 hours after training.
source: Translin KO mice explored the displaced object (DO) significantly less than WT littermates 24 hr after training (C; t-test, p=0.004)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C with statistical analysis (t-test, p=0.004)

claim: Translin knockout mice explored the displaced object similarly to wildtype littermates 1 hour after training.
source: while explored DO similar to WT littermates 1 hr after training (D; t-test, p=0.5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis (t-test, p=0.5)

claim: Preference for the displaced object was significantly reduced in translin knockout mice compared to wildtype littermates 24 hours after training.
source: Compared to WT littermates, preference for the displaced object was significantly reduced in translin KO mice (Figure 1D; WT: 52.3 ± 1.8%, n = 9; KO: 42.6 ± 2.4%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with quantitative measurements

claim: 1 hour short-term memory was unaffected in translin knockout mice.
source: However, 1 hr short-term memory was unaffected in translin KO mice (Figure 1C; WT: 44.4 ± 1.5%; KO: 41.5 ± 4%)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C with quantitative measurements

claim: Translin knockout mice are able to acquire relevant information but have deficits in memory consolidation.
source: However, 1 hr short-term memory was unaffected in translin KO mice (Figure 1C; WT: 44.4 ± 1.5%; KO: 41.5 ± 4%), suggesting that translin KO mice are able to acquire relevant information, but have deficits in memory consolidation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that short-term memory is intact while long-term memory is impaired

claim: Translin knockout mice exhibit unaltered exploratory behavior in an open field.
source: In line with previous findings that translin KO mice exhibit unaltered exploratory behavior in an open field (Stein et al., 2006), the total object exploration time during training and testing did not differ across groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stein et al., 2006 and experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Total object exploration time during training and testing did not differ between translin knockout and wildtype mice.
source: In line with previous findings that translin KO mice exhibit unaltered exploratory behavior in an open field (Stein et al., 2006), the total object exploration time during training and testing did not differ across groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Translin/trax is critical for heterosynaptic strengthening of short-lived potentiation and long-term associative memory formation.
source: Overall, these data indicate that translin/trax is critical for heterosynaptic strengthening of short-lived potentiation and long-term associative memory formation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations including synaptic tagging and behavioral data

claim: Nearly all identified puncta for trax co-localized with puncta for GW182 in dendrites.
source: Immunostaining of primary hippocampal neurons revealed that nearly all identified puncta for trax, the catalytic subunit of translin/trax (Liu et al., 2009), co-localized with puncta for GW182, a P-body marker, in dendrites.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data and citation to Liu et al., 2009

claim: Many GW182-positive puncta were not trax-positive.
source: Conversely, many GW182-positive puncta were not trax-positive.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining observations

claim: Translin/trax is well-positioned to regulate microRNA-mediated translational silencing.
source: Together with previous findings that translin/trax degrades microRNAs, these data indicate that translin/trax is well-positioned to regulate microRNA-mediated translational silencing (Figure 2).
evidence: Inferred from co-localization data and previous findings about translin/trax function

claim: Translin knockout mice show significant increases in the levels of let-7c-5p, miR-125b-5p, miR-128-3p, and miR-9-3p in the hippocampus 30 minutes following training.
source: Compared to WT littermates, translin KO mice show significant increases in the levels of let-7c-5p, miR-125b-5p, miR-128–3p, and miR-9–3p in the hippocampus 30 min following training.
evidence: Supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis

claim: There was no difference in candidate microRNA levels between translin knockout mice and wildtype littermates kept under homecage conditions.
source: Surprisingly, however, there was no difference across candidate microRNAs between translin KO mice and WT littermates kept under homecage conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Let-7c-5p, miR-125b-5p, miR-128-3p, and miR-9-3p are brain enriched and implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: These microRNAs are brain enriched and implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, Alzheimer's Disease and anxiety (Edbauer et al., 2010; Lukiw, 2007; Muiños-Gimeno et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Edbauer et al., 2010; Lukiw, 2007; Muiños-Gimeno et al., 2009

claim: miR-409-3p levels in the hippocampus were increased in translin knockout mice both after training and in home cage conditions.
source: In contrast, miR-409–3p was not a learning specific target of translin/trax as its levels in the hippocampus were increased in translin KO mice both after training and in home cage conditions (p=0.00009 and p=0.03, respectively; data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (p=0.00009 and p=0.03)

claim: Translin/trax mediates rapid degradation of selected microRNAs after learning in vivo.
source: These data suggest that translin/trax mediates rapid degradation of selected microRNAs after learning in vivo, and could thereby reverse translational silencing of plasticity transcripts targeted by these microRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that specific microRNAs are elevated in translin KO mice only after training

claim: ACVR1C has the highest aggregate context score among the thirteen transcripts targeted by let-7c-5p, miR-125b-5p and miR-128-3p.
source: ACVR1C was of particular interest because it has the highest aggregate context score (Grimson et al., 2007) within this group (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis and citation to Grimson et al., 2007

claim: A fragment of the ACVR1C 3'UTR containing target sites for let-7c-5p and miR-128-3p produces robust silencing of a luciferase reporter in response to treatment with either of these microRNAs.
source: Consistent with their predicted context scores (Figure 3—source data 1), a fragment of the ACVR1C 3'UTR containing target sites for let-7c-5p and miR-128–3p produced robust silencing of a luciferase reporter in response to treatment with either of these microRNAs, but not to miR-125–5p (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4A and B with statistical analysis

claim: The ACVR1C 3'UTR fragment does not produce silencing in response to miR-125-5p treatment.
source: Consistent with their predicted context scores (Figure 3—source data 1), a fragment of the ACVR1C 3'UTR containing target sites for let-7c-5p and miR-128–3p produced robust silencing of a luciferase reporter in response to treatment with either of these microRNAs, but not to miR-125–5p (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis

claim: The luciferase activity of TRIM71 was suppressed by let-7c-5p and miR-125-5p, but not miR-128-3p.
source: The luciferase activity of the positive control TRIM71, which has target sites for let-7c-5p and miR-125–5p, was suppressed by let-7c-5p and miR-125–5p, but not miR-128–3p (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4C with statistical analysis

claim: The effects of let-7c-5p and miR-128-3p on luciferase activity were prevented by treatment with their inhibitors.
source: The effects of these microRNAs were prevented by the treatment with their inhibitors (Figure 4D) or mutating their target sites in the 3'UTR (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4D with statistical analysis

claim: The effects of let-7c-5p and miR-128-3p on luciferase activity were prevented by mutating their target sites in the 3'UTR.
source: The effects of these microRNAs were prevented by the treatment with their inhibitors (Figure 4D) or mutating their target sites in the 3'UTR (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4E with statistical analysis

claim: ACVR1C is subject to silencing directly by let-7c and miR-128-3p.
source: These studies confirm that ACVR1C is subject to silencing directly by let-7c and miR-128–3p.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from luciferase reporter assays

claim: Training increased translin protein levels in hippocampal synaptosomes 30 minutes after training.
source: Indeed, translin protein levels increased in hippocampal synaptosomes 30 min after training (Figure 5; home cage: 100 ± 7.3%, training: 142 ± 10%).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5 with quantitative measurements and statistical analysis (t-test, p=0.01)

claim: Training increased synaptosomal ACVR1C protein levels in wildtype littermates but not in mice lacking translin/trax.
source: Moreover, training increased synaptosomal ACVR1C protein levels in WT littermates, but not in mice lacking translin/trax, although baseline ACVR1C levels were similar between the groups (Figure 5; WThomecage: 100 ± 8.7%, WTtraining: 198.8 ± 28.6%; KOhomecage: 102 ± 18.4%, KOtraining: 106.4 ± 8.7%).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5 with quantitative measurements and statistical analysis

claim: Baseline ACVR1C levels were similar between wildtype and translin knockout mice.
source: Moreover, training increased synaptosomal ACVR1C protein levels in WT littermates, but not in mice lacking translin/trax, although baseline ACVR1C levels were similar between the groups (Figure 5; WThomecage: 100 ± 8.7%, WTtraining: 198.8 ± 28.6%; KOhomecage: 102 ± 18.4%, KOtraining: 106.4 ± 8.7%).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5 with quantitative measurements

claim: Synaptosomal VANGL2 levels were unaffected by training or genotype.
source: Synaptosomal VANGL2 levels were unaffected by training or genotype (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5 with statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA: genotype, F(1,16) = 0.06, p=0.8; training, F(1,16) = 0.3, p=0.6)

claim: Increased synaptic expression of ACVR1C protein following training requires translin/trax.
source: Thus, increased synaptic expression of ACVR1C protein following training requires translin/trax.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Western blot data showing training-induced ACVR1C upregulation in WT but not KO mice

claim: Training induces synaptic ACVR1C expression by translin-mediated reversal of microRNA silencing of this transcript.
source: Together with luciferase studies, these findings reveal that training induces synaptic ACVR1C expression by translin-mediated reversal of microRNA silencing of this transcript.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including luciferase assays and Western blot data

claim: SB431542 treatment did not alter long-lasting potentiation in pathway S1.
source: We found that SB431542 did not alter long-lasting potentiation in pathway S1 (Figure 6A1)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6A1 with statistical analysis (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,8) = 0.3, p=0.6)

claim: SB431542 blocked heterosynaptic strengthening of pathway S2 in hippocampal slices from wildtype mice.
source: We found that SB431542 did not alter long-lasting potentiation in pathway S1 (Figure 6A1), but blocked heterosynaptic strengthening of pathway S2 (Figure 6A2) in hippocampal slices from WT mice.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6A2 with statistical analysis (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,8) = 13.9, p=0.007)

claim: SB431542 treatment did not alter baseline synaptic responses in pathway S2.
source: Consistent with previous findings that activin signaling is not required for basal synaptic transmission (Ageta et al., 2010), SB431542 treatment did not alter baseline synaptic responses in pathway S2 (Figure 6A2).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6A2 and citation to Ageta et al., 2010

claim: Treatment with SB431542 during the last 1 hour of recordings impaired the maintenance phase of S2 potentiation.
source: Moreover, treatment with SB431542 during the last 1 hr of the recordings impaired the maintenance phase of S2 potentiation (Figure 6A3 and A4).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6A3 and A4 with statistical analysis (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,8) = 6.1, p=0.039)

claim: ACVR1C is required for persistent heterosynaptic strengthening of pathway S2.
source: Thus, these findings indicate that ACVR1C is required for persistent heterosynaptic strengthening of pathway S2 and is involved in post-tagging maintenance of this form of heterosynaptic plasticity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SB431542 treatment experiments

claim: ACVR1C is involved in post-tagging maintenance of heterosynaptic plasticity.
source: Thus, these findings indicate that ACVR1C is required for persistent heterosynaptic strengthening of pathway S2 and is involved in post-tagging maintenance of this form of heterosynaptic plasticity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from SB431542 treatment experiments showing impairment when applied during maintenance phase

claim: Intrahippocampal infusion of SB431542 immediately after training impaired long-term object-location memory 24 hours after training in wildtype mice.
source: Behaviorally, intrahippocampal infusion of SB431542 immediately after training impaired long-term object-location memory 24 hr after training in WT mice (Figure 6B2; vehicle: 52.1 ± 1.3%, SB 431542: 38.3 ± 1.3%).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6B2 with quantitative measurements and statistical analysis

claim: Intrahippocampal injection of SB431542 did not alter total object exploration time during training and testing.
source: Intrahippocampal injection of SB431542 did not alter the total object exploration time during training (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and testing (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; vehicle: 2.7 ± 0.3 s; SB431542: 2.9 ± 0.4 s).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and 1B with quantitative measurements

claim: Treatment with SB431542 had no inhibitory effect on object location memory in translin knockout mice.
source: Even though the preference for the displaced object displayed by the translin KO mice was above chance level or 33% (p=0.0005), treatment with SB431542 had no further inhibitory effect (Figure 6B2; vehicle: 40.6 ± 2.5%; SB431542: 40.1 ± 2.1%).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6B2 with quantitative measurements and statistical analysis

claim: The memory deficits observed in translin knockout mice result from ACVR1C dysregulation.
source: Together, these data indicate that the memory deficits observed in translin KO mice result from ACVR1C dysregulation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that SB431542 impairs memory in WT but not KO mice

claim: The level of virally expressed translin reached wildtype levels 15 to 20 days after injection.
source: The level of virally expressed translin reached WT levels 15 to 20 days after injection (Figure 7C; WT: 100 ± 15.9%, KO15day: 105.6 ± 30.3%, KO20day: 159.6 ± 24.4%).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7C with quantitative measurements and statistical analysis

claim: Viral translin expression restored trax levels by 20 days post-injection.
source: Viral translin expression also restored trax levels by 20 day post-injection (Figure 7D; WT littermates: 100 ± 14%, KO20day: 93.9 ± 12.4%).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D with quantitative measurements and statistical analysis

claim: Basal synaptic properties measured by input-output relationship were not affected by viral expression of either translin or eGFP.
source: Basal synaptic properties measured by the input-output relationship and PPF were not affected by viral expression of either translin or eGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; translin virus group: 3.6 ± 0.5, eGFP virus group: 3.5 ± 0.5, andFigure 1—figure supplement 1C; two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(1,10) = 0.2, p=0.6).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B with quantitative measurements

claim: Paired-pulse facilitation was not affected by viral expression of either translin or eGFP.
source: Basal synaptic properties measured by the input-output relationship and PPF were not affected by viral expression of either translin or eGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; translin virus group: 3.6 ± 0.5, eGFP virus group: 3.5 ± 0.5, andFigure 1—figure supplement 1C; two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(1,10) = 0.2, p=0.6).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C with statistical analysis (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(1,10) = 0.2, p=0.6)

claim: Viral expression of translin in the hippocampus of adult translin knockout mice rescued the deficits in synaptic tagging.
source: We found that the viral expression of translin in the hippocampus of adult translin KO mice rescued the deficits in synaptic tagging (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7E with statistical analysis (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,6) = 29.3, p=0.002)

claim: Adult translin knockout mice expressing eGFP explored the displaced object significantly less than wildtype littermates 24 hours after training.
source: Adult translin KO mice expressing eGFP explored the DO significantly less than WT littermates 24 hr after training.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7F2 with statistical analysis

claim: The behavior of adult translin knockout mice expressing translin in excitatory neurons was similar to that of wildtype littermates.
source: However, the behavior of adult translin KO mice expressing translin in excitatory neurons was similar to that of WT littermates or WT littermates expressing eGFP.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7F2 with statistical analysis

claim: Viral eGFP expression did not alter the behavior of wildtype littermates.
source: Viral eGFP expression did not alter the behavior of WT littermates (one-way ANOVA, F(3,29) = 13.9, p=0.00001, Dunnett's post hoc test, WTeGFP vs. KOeGFP: p=0.0001, WTeGFP vs. KOtranslin: p=0.5, WTeGFP vs. WT: p=0.9).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(3,29) = 13.9, p=0.00001)

claim: The viral restoration of translin/trax levels in adult excitatory neurons in the hippocampus rescued the memory deficits in knockout mice.
source: The viral restoration of translin/trax levels in adult excitatory neurons in the hippocampus rescued the memory deficits in KO mice (Figure 7F2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7F2 with statistical analysis

claim: The lack of an effect of eGFP expression on the behavior of wildtype mice indicates that viral infection was not responsible for the observed rescue.
source: The lack of an effect of eGFP expression on the behavior of WT mice indicates that viral infection was not responsible for the observed rescue (Figure 7F2).
evidence: Inferred from control experiment showing no effect of eGFP virus on WT behavior

claim: No difference was observed between male and female mice during object location memory task.
source: In contrast to previous findings that male KO mice show increased escape latency during trainings for the water maze task while female KO mice display enhanced freezing during fear memory testing (Stein et al., 2006), no difference was observed between male and female during object location memory task (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and citation to Stein et al., 2006

claim: The function of translin/trax in adult excitatory neurons is critical for heterosynaptic strengthening of short-lived potentiation and long-term memory formation.
source: Therefore, the function of translin/trax in adult excitatory neurons is critical for heterosynaptic strengthening of short-lived potentiation and long-term memory formation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from viral rescue experiments

claim: The observed deficits were not due to compensatory developmental changes caused by constitutive deletion of the translin gene.
source: Moreover, this viral reinstatement approach confirms that the observed deficits were not due to compensatory developmental changes caused by constitutive deletion of the translin gene.
evidence: Inferred from the fact that viral restoration in adult mice rescues the phenotype

claim: Mice lacking translin/trax display increased levels of several microRNAs following learning, not at baseline.
source: Unlike conventional studies focusing on basal genetic alterations leading to defective phenotypes, we found that mice lacking translin/trax display increased levels of several microRNAs following learning, not at baseline.
evidence: Supported by real-time RT-PCR data comparing homecage and post-training conditions

claim: The lack of translin/trax abolishes learning-induced synaptic upregulation of ACVR1C.
source: Unlike conventional studies focusing on basal genetic alterations leading to defective phenotypes, we found that mice lacking translin/trax display increased levels of several microRNAs following learning, not at baseline. These microRNAs suppress the expression of the activin receptor ACVR1C, and the lack of translin/trax abolishes learning-induced synaptic upregulation of ACVR1C.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing no training-induced ACVR1C upregulation in KO mice

claim: Inhibition of ACVR1C after synaptic stimulation or learning phenocopies the defects in synaptic plasticity or memory displayed by translin knockout mice.
source: Finally, inhibition of ACVR1C after synaptic stimulation or learning phenocopies the defects in synaptic plasticity or memory displayed by translin KO mice.
evidence: Supported by SB431542 treatment experiments showing similar deficits to KO mice

claim: Learning or synaptic stimulation engages translin/trax to reverse silencing of ACVR1C.
source: Taken together, these findings provide compelling evidence for a novel pathway underlying long-term plasticity and memory, in which learning or synaptic stimulation engages translin/trax to reverse silencing of ACVR1C.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including microRNA, protein expression, and functional studies

claim: Absence of translin/trax does not impact high frequency stimulation-induced long-lasting potentiation.
source: Absence of translin/trax does not impact high frequency stimulation-induced long-lasting potentiation, but does cause selective impairment in heterosynaptic tagging.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data showing normal 4-train LTP in pathway S1

claim: Absence of translin/trax causes selective impairment in heterosynaptic tagging.
source: Absence of translin/trax does not impact high frequency stimulation-induced long-lasting potentiation, but does cause selective impairment in heterosynaptic tagging.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data showing impaired S2 potentiation

claim: Both male and female translin knockout mice exhibit long-term memory deficits in an object-location task.
source: In contrast, we found in this study that both male and female translin KO mice exhibit long-term memory deficits in an object-location task.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing no gender difference in the phenotype

claim: Inhibition of ACVR1C selectively blocks the maintenance of synaptic tagging and object-location memory.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of ACVR1C, a target of translin/trax identified in the present study, selectively blocks the maintenance of synaptic tagging and object-location memory.
evidence: Supported by SB431542 treatment experiments showing effects on maintenance phase

claim: Object-location memory may depend on the plasticity processes that mediate heterosynaptic plasticity.
source: Thus, object-location memory, in which mice integrate information about object identity and spatial location, may depend on the plasticity processes that mediate heterosynaptic plasticity.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the parallel deficits in heterosynaptic plasticity and object-location memory

claim: ACVR1C is a key plasticity protein that is critical for heterosynaptic strengthening of short-lived plasticity and long-term memory.
source: This study is the first to show that ACVR1C is a key plasticity protein that is critical for heterosynaptic strengthening of short-lived plasticity and long-term memory
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental approaches including pharmacological inhibition and genetic studies

claim: Activin mRNA is upregulated by stimuli that induce long-term potentiation.
source: Activin mRNA is upregulated by stimuli that induce long-term potentiation (Inokuchi et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citation to Inokuchi et al., 1996

claim: Activin treatment facilitates short-lived potentiation.
source: and activin treatment facilitates short-lived potentiation (Ageta et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ageta et al., 2010

claim: Activin signaling is required for long-term memory formation.
source: Furthermore, activin signaling is required for long-term memory formation (Ageta et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ageta et al., 2010

claim: ACVR1C blockade selectively affects the maintenance of strengthened short-lived plasticity.
source: Interestingly, we find that ACVR1C blockade selectively affects the maintenance of strengthened short-lived plasticity, a finding that distinguishes ACVR1C from other plasticity proteins postulated to be involved in synaptic tagging such as PKMζ and BDNF (Barco et al., 2005; Sajikumar et al., 2009; Yao et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Barco et al., 2005; Sajikumar et al., 2009; Yao et al., 2008

claim: Treatment with ZIP impairs maintenance of both long-lasting plasticity and strengthened short-lived plasticity.
source: Although recent studies challenge the specificity of ZIP peptide in blocking PKMζ (Volk et al., 2013), treatment with ZIP impairs maintenance of both long-lasting plasticity and strengthened short-lived plasticity (Sajikumar et al., 2009; Tsokas et al., 2016; Yao et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Volk et al., 2013; Sajikumar et al., 2009; Tsokas et al., 2016; Yao et al., 2008

claim: Deletion of BDNF blocks both induction and maintenance of strengthened short-lived plasticity.
source: Additionally, deletion of BDNF blocks both induction and maintenance of strengthened short-lived plasticity (Barco et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barco et al., 2005

claim: The translin/trax/ACVR1C pathway is a new critical component of the molecular machinery mediating the maintenance of heterosynaptic plasticity and memory.
source: Overall, our results reveal the translin/trax/ACVR1C pathway as a new critical component of the molecular machinery mediating the maintenance of heterosynaptic plasticity and memory.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from all experimental findings in the study

claim: Phosphorylation of translin changes its RNA-binding affinity.
source: Because phosphorylation of translin changes its RNA-binding affinity (Kwon and Hecht, 1993)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kwon and Hecht, 1993

claim: Translin binds actin.
source: and translin binds actin (Wu et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 1999

claim: Synaptic tags could regulate the activity or localization of translin/trax, leading to reversal of translational silencing of ACVR1C at synapses receiving strong input.
source: it is plausible that synaptic tags could regulate the activity or localization of translin/trax, leading to reversal of translational silencing of ACVR1C at synapses receiving strong input.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on known properties of translin and synaptic tagging models

claim: Learning increases translin levels in synaptosomes.
source: Indeed, we find that learning increases translin levels in synaptosomes supporting the view that it is recruited to the synapse after learning.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing increased synaptosomal translin after training

claim: Newly expressed ACVR1C could be captured by tags generated at weakly activated synapses.
source: Newly expressed ACVR1C could then be captured by tags generated at weakly activated synapses.
evidence: Speculative mechanism consistent with synaptic tagging models

claim: Activin is able to enhance synaptic contacts and spine growth via a process that requires CaMKII, PKA, ERK, and actin dynamics.
